_comment: Role materials for the Creative Negotiations sales-job scenario. Edit this file (and the scenario it links to) to change what participants see and how offers are scored; the app reloads it at every game start, no redeploy needed. `roles` follows the Empirica loader's format (one role per file). `scenario_url` points at the scorer's scenario JSON (issues, ranges, payoffs for both roles) used by server/src/score_offer/score_offer.py. `scorer_role` is the role name inside that scenario.

roles.narrative:
**RECRUITER** **ROLE INFORMATION** You are an ambitious Recruiter at a young company negotiating with a promising sales candidate. You care about making a strong hire, but filling the role isn't all that matters. You want to control costs, get the new hire productive quickly, keep the team working well, and avoid commitments that leave the company exposed if the hire does not work out. Your objective is to reach an agreement with the highest total score you can, while recognizing that the Candidate has priorities of their own that may conflict with yours. Every complete offer must include three terms: **salary**, a **starting date**, and a **personal budget for work expenses** such as client travel, meals, and lodging (but not take-home pay!). You prefer a lower salary and budget and an earlier start. • Annual salary may range from $20,000 to $80,000: $20,000 gives you +2 points,
$40,000 gives you 0, and $80,000 gives you −2. • Starting dates may range from 1 May to 30 September: 1 May gives you +2,
around 16 July gives you 0, and 30 September gives you −2. • The personal budget may range from $1,000 to $20,000: $1,000 gives you +2,
$10,500 gives you 0, and $20,000 gives you −2. The platform calculates intermediate scores automatically. For example, a $7,000 budget is worth about +0.74 points to you. You do not need to calculate this yourself. These headline contract terms are easy to put numbers on. However, the interview also left you thinking about what hiring this person would actually involve, what the Candidate might ask for, and what other terms could benefit the company. **Background Information** Looking over your notes, you think about the company's usual 3-month probation period and 3-year contract. Those arrangements seem sensible. Each is worth 0 points to you. Still, the sales manager's description of the Candidate as “bright but raw” makes you cautious about committing too much before seeing how they perform. • A longer probation gives the company more protection. For probation, no probation is worth −1 point to you and 6 months are worth +1. • Contract length works in the other direction: 2 years are worth +1 point to you and 4 years are worth −1. The two terms are scored separately, with proportional points for values in between. You also remember the Candidate's interest when you described the external professional training program and experienced employees who sometimes mentor new hires. Good development can turn a risky appointment into a strong performer and reflect well on your ability to spot talent. The Candidate was also curious about professional associations and recruitment fairs. Association sponsorship would cost the company money; a recruitment-fair role could help attract future candidates. Other parts of the conversation suggested different possibilities. • The Candidate was personable and might be good at organizing occasional team events. • Their sales work could provide material for LinkedIn posts and other public communications. • … Conference presentations sounded less useful. Your manager sees them as costly distractions, and the Candidate did not seem eager to spend evenings preparing slides. The Candidate's question about waiving the standard non-compete also stayed with you. • You understand why future flexibility matters to them. • But if they later leave for a competitor with knowledge of your clients, colleagues may ask why you gave up that protection. • You want the new hire to develop and succeed without leaving the company unnecessarily exposed. The interview contained small details and examples rather than a neat menu of contract features. Some may simply be background. Others could become useful terms if you connect them to what matters to the company. **Your Task** Negotiate with the Candidate by making offers in plain, ordinary language, as if you were writing them a short message. Every complete offer must include salary, a personal work-expense budget, and a starting date. You decide what else is worth discussing and when to raise it. **For example:** “I propose a salary of [amount], a personal work-expense budget of [amount], and a starting date of [date], together with [list any job features you want to bring up].” Use your own values and wording. **Your score** is private and **translates** directly into the **bonus payment you** can **earn** from this task. • You may propose an offer worth zero or less to you, but you can accept only an offer worth more than zero to you. • An agreement requires both parties to accept the same offer, with a positive total score for you and the Candidate. **Important notes on offers and scoring** 1. Without a deal, you will keep recruiting while the existing team covers the vacancy. This fallback is worth 0 points. 2. The researchers set the scoring rules in advance, and the platform calculates points automatically; you do not assign or calculate points yourself. 3. Each additional contract feature introduced in the negotiation is worth **between** −1 and +1 points to you, based on the interests in your role. Its value to the Candidate may differ. 4. **You are not limited to the job features described or suggested here. You may creatively introduce other plausible contract features or job arrangements.** 5. Some features you introduce may not fit the situation and will be worth 0 points. But that doesn't mean you should hold back on creative and thoughtful ideas!
roles.BATNA: If you do not reach an agreement, you receive 0 points. An agreement only counts if the total score is above zero for both parties.

tips:
Negotiation is a skill you can get better at with practice. At its core, it is about making choices when people want different things, with each person’s decision affecting what the others get out of the deal. The good news is that a few basic ideas go a long way.

One of the most important ideas is knowing your best alternative to negotiating an agreement, or your BATNA. This is your realistic fallback plan outside the negotiation. Knowing what that alternative is actually worth helps protect you from accepting an agreement that leaves you worse off than walking away. A simple rule follows from this: never accept a deal worse than your BATNA.

Another key idea is that some negotiations can be win-win. This happens when people value different issues differently. If something matters a lot to you but not as much to the other person, you may be able to trade it for something you care about more. In practice, this means focusing less on “splitting the difference” and more on learning what the other person really wants, so you can make smart tradeoffs that leave both of you better off.

A final tip is that win-win outcomes become easier to achieve when everyone knows what matters most to each party . So try to be clear about what you care about, and how these interests translate to what you want across each issue under negotiation. At the same time, listen closely to what the other person cares about. Knowing this is what will make such smart, win-win tradeoffs possible.
